title: The Renaissance revival: Hermes before Plato
desc: In 1463 a dying Medici made his translator shelve Plato to do Hermes first. The century that followed ran on a dating error — a productive one.
tldr: In 1463, Cosimo de' Medici — dying, with Plato's complete works on his translator's desk — ordered Marsilio Ficino to translate Hermes first. That queue-jump captures the whole Renaissance revival: the Hermetica were believed to be older than Moses, so they outranked Plato. The belief was a dating error; the error powered 150 years of philosophy and magic; and when one philologist corrected it in 1614, Hermeticism went on living for another three centuries anyway.
body:
Florence, 1463. Cosimo de’ Medici is dying, and on Marsilio Ficino’s desk sits the complete works of Plato, waiting to enter Latin for the first time in a thousand years. A monk, Leonardo da Pistoia, has recently arrived from Macedonia carrying a Greek manuscript of the Corpus Hermeticum. Cosimo’s order: stop the Plato. Do Hermes first — he wants to read him before he dies. Ficino delivers the translation in 1463, a year before Cosimo’s death; printed in 1471 as the Pimander, it becomes one of the best-selling philosophical books of the era. Hold that image: the Renaissance made Plato wait for Hermes. Everything in this step explains why.

The licence: prisca theologia

The reason was chronology. Ficino called Hermes “the first author of theology”, head of a succession running through Orpheus and Pythagoras down to Plato — the doctrine of prisca theologia, an ancient wisdom flowing toward Christianity. Because the Hermetica were believed roughly contemporary with Moses, they seemed to anticipate Genesis and the Gospel of John — which made quoting Hermes not heresy but evidence. That belief was the operating licence of the whole revival: it let Christian scholars practise astral magic and read pagan revelation as prophecy. It was also, as we’ll see, wrong.

The cast

Under that licence, a remarkable cast went to work. Pico della Mirandola posted 900 theses for public debate in 1486 and folded Jewish Kabbalah into the synthesis — though he actually preferred Orphic and Chaldean sources and downplayed the Hermetica. Lodovico Lazzarelli completed Ficino’s corpus by translating the treatises Ficino’s manuscript lacked — and, having met a street prophet he took for Hermes reborn, actually lived the Hermetic rebirth the texts describe. Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa distilled the era’s magic into De occulta philosophia (printed 1533), the most comprehensive manual of occult philosophy ever assembled — after publishing, three years earlier, a book arguing all sciences are vanity. In Elizabethan England, John Dee compressed the cosmos into a single glyph (Monas Hieroglyphica, 1564) and spent his later years transcribing conversations with angels.

1614: the audit

Then a philologist checked the dates. Isaac Casaubon, in a 1614 polemic against Catholic church history, showed that the Corpus’s Greek is post-classical — Hellenistic vocabulary, echoes of Plato and Scripture — and placed the texts in the early Christian centuries. The pre-Mosaic Hermes evaporated; the chronology under prisca theologia collapsed. One footnote of honesty: Nag Hammadi and demotic parallels have since shown genuine Egyptian material inside those late Greek texts. Casaubon was right about the date and too quick about the “forgery”.

The tradition that outlived its death

Here is the twist worth keeping: Hermeticism survived its own debunking by 300 years. Robert Fludd built his macrocosm–microcosm system after 1614 as if nothing had happened; Athanasius Kircher was still channelling Hermes in 1652; Ralph Cudworth argued in 1678 that late texts could preserve older oral tradition; and in 1888 a new occult order put the refuted name on its front door: the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn. Philology corrected a date. It could not kill a tradition. What that tradition did in the laboratory — alchemy, the Great Work — is step 09.
facts: 1463: Cosimo orders Hermes translated before Plato
Ficino's Pimander, printed 1471; dozens of editions by 1600
Prisca theologia — Hermes believed older than Moses
Casaubon 1614: the Greek is post-classical, texts early CE
faq: Where is Giordano Bruno in this story?
Deliberately in a footnote: the 'Hermetic martyr' image owes more to 1960s historiography (Frances Yates) and the 1889 monument than to the trial record. He has his own card — myths included.
Did Casaubon set out to destroy Hermeticism?

No — his 1614 book was Protestant source-criticism aimed at Cardinal Baronius's church history. The Hermetic redating was a demolition performed in passing, which makes it better, not worse, as philology.
So was the Renaissance revival built on nothing?
It was built on a wrong date attached to real ancient texts. The texts remain genuinely late-antique — and the philosophy, art and science the error licensed were entirely real.
